steps.title: Verbs of the senses
steps.html:
Noticing versus choosing. See and hear happen to you: you do not decide to do them, and they are rarely used in continuous tenses (I see the plate, not I am seeing the plate). Look at, watch and listen to are things you choose to do, and they are perfectly normal in continuous tenses.

Look at or watch? You look at a thing that is still — a photograph, a label, a plate. You watch something that happens or moves — a film, a chef, a match, people eating crisps. A screen is watched; a picture is looked at.

Prepositions. Look at, gaze at, stare at, glance at, glare at, listen to — all take one. See, hear, watch, notice and observe take a direct object with no preposition at all.

After the verb. Watch / see / hear + object + bare infinitive means you experienced the complete event: I heard him say it. The same verbs + object + -ing means you caught it in progress: I heard him saying it.

Linking verbs. Look, taste, smell, sound and feel can describe a quality, and then they take an adjective: it tastes salty, it looks fresh, that sounds terrible. With like they take a noun: it tastes like seaweed.

Speaking quietly. Whisper uses breath instead of voice; murmur is a low, unclear sound. Both can take a direct object: she whispered my name, he murmured something.

steps.title: The commonest errors at this level
steps.html:
• I am seeing a film tonight when watching is meant.
  • Listen the music — listen always needs to.
  • Watch at the screen — watch takes no preposition.
  • It tastes well — use the adjective: it tastes good.
  • Distinguish A and B — use between A and B.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
You smell it from the corner of the street, which is the point: an aroma of hot oil, cumin and something sweet underneath, arriving thirty seconds before you can see where it comes from. By the time I reached the stall I had already decided to buy whatever it was.

The sound is the second thing. The man was working two pans at once, and each time he dropped a new batch in, the oil made a noise you could hear across the road. I stood and watched him for four or five minutes. He glanced at me twice, said nothing, and murmured something to the woman taking the money that made her laugh.

On the plate it looked less impressive than it smelt: eight small brown parcels, slightly uneven, on a piece of paper going transparent at the edges. What you notice is the surface, which is not smooth but rough and blistered. I could hear the crunch before I tasted anything, and I now know from the research that this is half of what I thought the flavour was.

Then the taste, which was salty first, savoury underneath, and faintly sour at the very end, from something in the sauce I could not distinguish from vinegar and probably was not. It tasted like nothing I had eaten at home. They were samsa, from a stall outside the bus station, and I have thought about them for two years.
